data.title: SA analyst: Volatility could fade, but markets must stabilize first
data.description:
Wall Street endured a steep selloff Friday, with technology stocks leading a broad market retreat that left major indexes facing one of their worst weekly performances in quite some time.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJI) fell -1.9%, while the S&P 500 (SP500) dropped -3.6% and the Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) plunged -5.2%. 

Seeking Alpha analyst Alex King of Cestrian Capital Research acknowledged the difficult stretch for bullish investors but suggested several factors could help markets stabilize in the coming week. 

King pointed to the possibility that the CBOE Volatility Index’s recent spike could quickly reverse, while declining Treasury yields may signal improving conditions for equities. He also cited monthly options expiration as a potential contributor to Friday’s market turbulence. 

“This last week has tested the patience, and likely the resources, of the most zoomed-out bulls,” King stated. However, he cautioned against assuming the worst is over, emphasizing that market price action remains the most important signal. 

“But as always the only thing that matters is price; and price has yet to stabilize in the indices,” he added. King noted that falling yields have supported his bullish outlook on bonds, even as equity markets continue to struggle.

data.title: Sony pulls out of talks with Tishman Speyer on leasing anchor space at new skyscraper - report
data.description:
Sony Group (SONY) (SONY:CA) (SNEJF) has pulled out of negotiations to become an anchor tenant at a new skyscraper in New York City's Hudson Yards, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg News.

Sony was in talks for a lease with the real estate developer Tishman Speyer as recently as last month, a recent report by the Commercial Observer had noted.

Tishman Speyer is now left without a lease for an anchor space while approaching the final stages of receiving an approval for a key tax break, said the sources, who asked not to be named discussing private negotiations.

data.title: Nasdaq plummets more than -5% and the S&P 500 ends in correction territory
data.description:
Wall Street’s major averages plummeted lower on Friday and finished deep in the red as the tech selloff intensified. 

The blue-chip Dow (DJI) finished -1.9%, the benchmark S&P 500 (SP500) closed -3.6%, and the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) ended -5.2%. 

From a sector-by-sector basis, 10 of the 11 segments concluded lower, with info tech leading the way down, while consumer staples was the strongest area.

“This last week has tested the patience, and likely the resources, of the most zoomed-out bulls.  Since the entire Internet is filled with victory laps from bears and cope from bulls, for now I think we can just say; likely the VIX spike collapses next week, likely the drop in yields today portends coming strength in equities, and likely monthly opex today has added to the witches’ brew," Seeking Alpha analyst Alex King of Cestrian Capital Research stated.

Sentiment toward artificial intelligence stocks remained under heavy pressure after Anthropic's (ANT) much-anticipated public market debut failed to provide the boost investors had hoped for, extending a volatile week for equities. 

The U.S. 2-year Treasury yield (US2Y) dropped 13 basis points to 4.63%, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield (US10Y) shifted down 12 basis points to 4.92%, and the U.S. 30-year Treasury yield (US30Y) moved down 9 basis points to 5.31%. 

As for other stocks that were on the move, shares of Fair Isaac Corp. (FICO) advanced +2.5%, while shares of Sandisk (SNDK) dropped -15.9%.

data.title: Valvoline cut to Sell equivalent at J.P. Morgan as price-driven growth seen moderating
data.description:
Valvoline (VVV) slipped 1.1% in Friday's trading as J.P. Morgan downgraded the second-largest U.S. quick-change motor oil chain, saying price-driven growth could moderate in the long run, given that nearly 80% of the company's oil changes are already in the synthetic, or "premium," category.

Valvoline (VVV) continues to build and acquire new stores to extend its growth momentum asa larger percentage of its store network matures, but this aggressive store expansion strategy is capital intensive and limits free cash flow generation, JPM analyst Jeffrey Zekauskas said.

A decrease in oil prices from an opening of the Strait of Hormuz would provide a meaningfulbenefit to margins over time by lowering raw material costs, and Zekauskas said such a possibility is part of a core long-term investment thesis for the company; conversely, higher oil prices would most likely pressure volumes and margins.

Valvoline's (VVV) long-term outlook may also be pressured by higher electric vehicle adoption, which reduces demand for traditional oil-change services, the analyst said.

data.title: Kobeissi isn’t buying the AI bubble crash narrative
data.description:
The Kobeissi Letter argued Friday that the $6T market cap erasure across U.S. equities over the last 45 days reflects a normal tech (XLK) correction driven by extreme, polarized sentiment rather than the popping of an artificial intelligence (AIQ) bubble.

Since the S&P 500 (SPY) (VOO) hit its record high on Oct. 6, U.S. stocks have lost an average of $225B per day over 31 straight trading sessions, Kobeissi noted in an article posted on X. The 45-day stretch has absorbed Iran War headlines, Q3 earnings anxiety, concerns over AI capital expenditures and free cash flow, the October Fed meeting, the midterm elections, and the Nvidia (NVDA) controversy.

Compounding the stress, Anthropic's (ANT) record-shattering initial public offering raised over $100B—with institutional demand hitting $400B and retail orders at $100B—draining market liquidity. Hedge funds posted their largest six-week net tech outflow in over a decade, while the Wall Street fear gauge (VIX) surged more than 100% from its October low.

The selloff started with legitimate fears about Big Tech's AI spending spree. Combined capital expenditures from Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL), Meta (META), and Microsoft (MSFT) rose $36.9B in Q3 to a record $201.9B—up 356% since Q1 2024, with $1.6T deployed over three years, Kobeissi noted. Meanwhile, S&P 500 companies have reported 31.9% year-over-year EPS growth in Q3, the strongest in at least four years, with actual earnings beating estimates for 13 consecutive quarters.

Clarity on return on investment should emerge by Q1/Q2 2027, Kobeissi said.

Political shifts added fuel. The Democrats' midterm sweep effectively ended what Kobeissi calls the "Trump Put"—the market's confidence that President Donald Trump would intervene during volatility. A Nov. 4 congressional call for an AI ban rattled sentiment further. Kobeissi dismisses outright ban fears as geopolitically untenable—tantamount to surrendering the AI race to China (MCHI)—though higher corporate bond yields and Federal Reserve Chair Warsh's hawkish stance compound near-term pressure.

With valuations collapsing to extremes—Nvidia's forward price-to-earnings multiple has dropped to just 9x—Kobeissi sees significant bearishness already priced in, creating a compelling risk-reward setup for high-quality tech names once liquidity returns—similar to the dip-buying rotation that followed April 2025.
